Fix \(P\in\mathcal M\), \(x\in\mathcal X\), and \(s,t\in\mathbb R\).  By
\(\mathrm{ass{:}strata}\), \(p_x>0\), so conditioning on \(X=x\) is
well defined.  From the definitions of the replicates,
\[
 e^{i(sS_1+tS_2)}=e^{i(s+t)A}e^{isU_1}e^{itU_2}.
\]
The independence in \(\mathrm{ass{:}error\text{-}latent\text{-}independence}\)
and \(\mathrm{ass{:}error\text{-}coordinate\text{-}independence}\) therefore
gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 F_x(s,t)
 &=E_P[e^{i(s+t)A}\mid X=x]E_P[e^{isU_1}]E_P[e^{itU_2}]\\
 &=\left\{\int_{\mathcal A}e^{i(s+t)a}f_x(a)\,da\right\}
      \phi_1(s)\phi_2(t)\\
 &=\widehat f_x(s+t)\phi_1(s)\phi_2(t).
\end{aligned}
\]
For the marked channel, the same two independence assumptions allow the
bounded mark to remain with the latent variables.  By the definitions of
\(m_x\) and \(q_x=m_xf_x\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
 G_x(s,t)
 &=E_P[Ye^{i(s+t)A}\mid X=x]E_P[e^{isU_1}]E_P[e^{itU_2}]\\
 &=\left\{\int_{\mathcal A}e^{i(s+t)a}
      E_P[Y\mid A=a,X=x]f_x(a)\,da\right\}\phi_1(s)\phi_2(t)\\
 &=\widehat q_x(s+t)\phi_1(s)\phi_2(t).
\end{aligned}
\]
The first integrand has modulus one.  For the second,
\(\mathrm{ass{:}consistency}\) and
\(\mathrm{ass{:}bounded\text{-}outcome}\) imply \(|Y|\le B_Y\) almost
surely, so every expectation exists.  Finally,
\(\mathrm{ass{:}compact\text{-}dose}\) justifies writing both integrals over
\(\mathcal A\).  This proves the two identities.

Let \(P^{(0)},P^{(1)}\in\mathcal M\) induce the same observed-data law, and
fix \(x\in\mathcal X\).  Assumption \(\mathrm{ass{:}strata}\) gives
\(p_x\ge p_{\min}>0\), so that common law determines \(F_x\) and \(G_x\).

We first derive a common nonvanishing neighborhood.  For either candidate
law, either \(j\in\{1,2\}\), and every real \(v\), the elementary bound
\(|e^{iz}-1|\le|z|\), H\"older's inequality, and
\(\mathrm{ass{:}error\text{-}moment}\) give
\[
\begin{aligned}
 |\phi_j(v)|
 &\ge1-|\phi_j(v)-1|\\
 &\ge1-E_P|e^{ivU_j}-1|\\
 &\ge1-|v|E_P|U_j|\\
 &\ge1-|v|\{E_P|U_j|^{q_e}\}^{1/q_e}
 \ge1-|v|M_e^{1/q_e}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus, with
\[
 \nu_*=(2M_e^{1/q_e})^{-1},\qquad c_*=\frac12,
 \qquad
 \delta=\min\left\{\frac{\nu_*}{2},\frac{1}{4B_A}\right\}>0,
\]
one has \(|\phi_j(v)|\ge c_*\) on \(|v|\le\nu_*\).  Moreover,
\(\mathrm{ass{:}compact\text{-}dose}\) and the fact that \(f_x\) is a
conditional density imply, for \(|w|\le2\delta\),
\[
 |\widehat f_x(w)-1|
 \le\int_{\mathcal A}|e^{iwa}-1|f_x(a)\,da
 \le B_A|w|\le\frac12.
\]
Hence \(|\widehat f_x(w)|\ge1/2\).  If \(|u|,|t|\le\delta\), the
factorization lemma yields
\[
 |F_x(u,t)|
 =|\widehat f_x(u+t)|\,|\phi_1(u)|\,|\phi_2(t)|
 \ge\frac18>0.                                                    \tag{1}
\]
This uses only the moment-derived neighborhood, not global nonvanishing.

The same H\"older estimate gives \(E_P|U_2|<\infty\), while compact dose support
gives \(|A|\le B_A\) almost surely.  Dominated differentiation is therefore
valid at \(t=0\).  Define the observed logarithmic derivative
\[
 D_x(u)=
 \frac{\left.\partial_tF_x(u,t)\right|_{t=0}}{F_x(u,0)},
 \qquad |u|\le\delta.
\]
Differentiating the factorization and using (1) gives
\[
 D_x(u)=\frac{\widehat f_x'(u)}{\widehat f_x(u)}
       +\frac{\phi_2'(0)}{\phi_2(0)}.
\]
Characteristic-function normalization gives \(\phi_2(0)=1\), and
\(\mathrm{ass{:}center\text{-}two}\) gives
\(\phi_2'(0)=iE_P[U_2]=0\).  Therefore every candidate satisfies
\[
 \widehat f_x'(u)=D_x(u)\widehat f_x(u),
 \qquad \widehat f_x(0)=1,
 \qquad |u|\le\delta.                                            \tag{2}
\]
For the two candidate laws, \(D_x\) is common.  Their transforms are
nonzero on this interval, so
\[
 R_x(u)=\frac{\widehat f_x^{(1)}(u)}{\widehat f_x^{(0)}(u)}
\]
satisfies \(R_x'(u)=0\) and \(R_x(0)=1\).  Consequently
\[
 \widehat f_x^{(1)}(u)=\widehat f_x^{(0)}(u),
 \qquad |u|\le\delta.                                            \tag{3}
\]
Only \(\phi_2\) was differentiated; no location normalization on \(U_1\)
has been used.

Let \(h=f_x^{(1)}-f_x^{(0)}\).  It is integrable and supported on
\(\mathcal A\).  For every \(z\in\mathbb C\), Tonelli's theorem gives
\[
 H(z):=\int_{\mathcal A}e^{iza}h(a)\,da
 =\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(iz)^k}{k!}
       \int_{\mathcal A}a^kh(a)\,da,                             \tag{4}
\]
because
\[
 \int_{\mathcal A}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}
 \frac{|za|^k}{k!}|h(a)|\,da
 \le e^{|z|B_A}\|h\|_1<\infty.
\]
Thus \(H\) is entire.  Equation (3) makes it zero on a real interval;
therefore every derivative at zero is zero, and the power series (4) gives
\(H(z)=0\) for every \(z\in\mathbb C\).

At \((u,0)\), the two channel factorizations and (1) give, for each
candidate,
\[
 \widehat q_x(u)=\widehat f_x(u)\frac{G_x(u,0)}{F_x(u,0)},
 \qquad |u|\le\delta.                                            \tag{5}
\]
The right-hand side is common, so the two marked transforms agree locally.
Furthermore, consistency and bounded outcomes imply \(|Y|\le B_Y\), hence
conditional Jensen's inequality and \(q_x=m_xf_x\) give
\[
 |q_x(a)|\le B_Yf_x(a)\quad\text{almost everywhere},
 \qquad \|q_x\|_1\le B_Y.                                       \tag{6}
\]
Each \(q_x\) is supported on \(\mathcal A\).  Applying (4) to the
difference of the two marked functions extends the local equality in (5) to
all complex arguments.

It remains only to turn equality of Fourier transforms into equality of the
underlying functions.  If \(h\) is either signal difference, then
\(h\in L^1(\mathbb R)\) and \(\widehat h(t)=0\) for every real \(t\).  For
\(\epsilon>0\), let
\[
 g_\epsilon(v)=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-1/2}e^{-v^2/(2\epsilon)}.
\]
The Gaussian integral and Fubini's theorem yield
\[
 (h*g_\epsilon)(a)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb R}
 e^{-ita}\widehat h(t)e^{-\epsilon t^2/2}\,dt=0.                \tag{7}
\]
Also
\[
 \|h*g_\epsilon-h\|_1
 \le\int g_\epsilon(v)\|h(\cdot-v)-h\|_1\,dv\longrightarrow0. \tag{8}
\]
Indeed, translation continuity follows first for compactly supported step
functions and then for arbitrary \(L^1\) functions by approximation; (8)
then follows by splitting at a fixed small \(|v|\) and using concentration of
\(g_\epsilon\) at zero.  Equations (7)--(8) imply \(h=0\) almost
everywhere.

Finally, \(\mathrm{ass{:}f\text{-}sobolev}\),
\(\mathrm{ass{:}q\text{-}sobolev}\), and \(\beta>1/2\) give unique
continuous representatives.  For either difference \(h\), Cauchy--Schwarz
gives
\[
 \int_{\mathbb R}|\widehat h(t)|\,dt
 \le
 \left\{\int(1+t^2)^\beta|\widehat h(t)|^2\,dt\right\}^{1/2}
 \left\{\int(1+t^2)^{-\beta}\,dt\right\}^{1/2}<\infty.
\]
Fourier inversion therefore yields a continuous representative, and two
continuous representatives equal almost everywhere only if they agree
everywhere.  Since \(x\) was arbitrary, the common observed law determines
every \(f_x\) and \(q_x\).  The proof remains valid when either error
characteristic function has an open zero set away from zero.

Fix \(P\in\mathcal M\), \(x\in\mathcal X\), and \(a\in I\).
Assumption \(\mathrm{ass{:}strata}\) gives \(p_x>0\).  Let
\((\mathcal V,\mathscr V)\), \(V\), and \(h\) be supplied by
\(\mathrm{ass{:}structural\text{-}response\text{-}surface}\), and define
\[
 K_x(C)=P(V\in C\mid X=x),
 \qquad
 g_x(u)=\int_{\mathcal V}h(u,x,v)\,K_x(dv),
 \quad u\in\mathcal A.                                          \tag{1}
\]
Joint measurability of \(h\) makes \(g_x\) measurable, and \(|h|\le B_Y\)
makes the integral finite.  The simultaneous probability-one equality in
the structural-response assumption, evaluated at the random coordinate
\(A\), and \(\mathrm{ass{:}consistency}\) give
\[
 Y=Y(A)=h(A,X,V)\quad\text{almost surely}.                        \tag{2}
\]
For every bounded Borel function \(\psi:\mathcal A\to\mathbb R\), the
conditional independence \(V\perp A\mid X\), the conditional density
\(f_x\), and (2) yield
\[
\begin{aligned}
 E_P[Y\psi(A)\mid X=x]
 &=E_P[h(A,x,V)\psi(A)\mid X=x]\\
 &=\int_{\mathcal A}\int_{\mathcal V}
 h(u,x,v)\psi(u)\,K_x(dv)f_x(u)\,du\\
 &=\int_{\mathcal A}g_x(u)\psi(u)f_x(u)\,du.                    \tag{3}
\end{aligned}
\]
By the defining property of \(m_x(u)=E_P[Y\mid A=u,X=x]\),
\[
 E_P[Y\psi(A)\mid X=x]
 =\int_{\mathcal A}m_x(u)\psi(u)f_x(u)\,du.                     \tag{4}
\]
Uniqueness of Radon--Nikodym derivatives in (3)--(4) gives
\[
 m_x(u)=g_x(u)
 \quad\text{for }f_x(u)\,du\text{-almost every }u.              \tag{5}
\]

We now remove the almost-everywhere qualification on \(I\).  By
\(\mathrm{ass{:}f\text{-}sobolev}\),
\(\mathrm{ass{:}q\text{-}sobolev}\), and \(\beta>1/2\), both \(f_x\)
and \(q_x\) possess continuous representatives.  Indeed, for either
function \(w\),
\[
 \int_{\mathbb R}|\widehat w(t)|\,dt
 \le
 \left\{\int(1+t^2)^\beta|\widehat w(t)|^2\,dt\right\}^{1/2}
 \left\{\int(1+t^2)^{-\beta}\,dt\right\}^{1/2}<\infty,          \tag{6}
\]
so Fourier inversion and dominated convergence give continuity.  Assumption
\(\mathrm{ass{:}denominator}\) gives \(f_x(u)\ge\kappa>0\) on \(I\), and
therefore
\[
 \widetilde m_x(u)=\frac{q_x(u)}{f_x(u)},\qquad u\in I,           \tag{7}
\]
is continuous.  Since \(q_x=m_xf_x\), (5) implies that
\(\widetilde m_x=g_x\) Lebesgue-almost everywhere on \(I\); here
\(f_x\ge\kappa\) converts an \(f_x(u)\,du\)-null set to a Lebesgue-null
set.  The structural representation in (1) gives
\[
 g_x(u)=E_P[Y(u)\mid X=x],                                       \tag{8}
\]
and \(\mathrm{ass{:}causal\text{-}mean\text{-}continuity}\) makes the
right-hand side continuous on \(I\).  Two continuous functions on an
interval that agree almost everywhere agree everywhere.  Hence, for every
\(u\in I\),
\[
 E_P[Y(u)\mid X=x]=\frac{q_x(u)}{f_x(u)}.                         \tag{9}
\]

Because \(\mathcal X\) is finite, the law of total expectation and (9) give
the equation-by-equation bridge
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \mu(a)
 &=E_P[Y(a)]                                                     \\
 &=\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}p_xE_P[Y(a)\mid X=x]                    \\
 &=\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}p_x\frac{q_x(a)}{f_x(a)}.               \tag{10}
\end{aligned}
\]
The first equality is the definition of the causal target, the second is
conditioning on the finite partition generated by \(X\), and the third is
(9).  Thus (10) is proved from the causal assumptions rather than imposed as
a definition.  Finally, each \(p_x\) is an observed marginal probability,
and \(\mathrm{thm{:}marked\text{-}cocycle\text{-}id}\) makes every \(f_x\)
and \(q_x\) a functional of \(P_{\mathrm{obs}}\).  Division in (10) is
legitimate by \(f_x\ge\kappa\) on \(I\), proving point identification.

Fix a sufficiently large \(n\).  Conditional on
\((X_i)_{i=1}^n\), \(\mathrm{ass{:}iid}\) makes the observations in each
nonempty cell independent with their law conditional on \(X=x\).  Each real
and imaginary part of a probability-channel summand lies in \([-1,1]\).
The structural-response condition, together with
\(\mathrm{ass{:}consistency}\), gives \(|Y|\le B_Y\), so the corresponding
parts of a marked-channel summand lie in \([-B_Y,B_Y]\).

The bounded-variable moment-generating-function calculation used in
\(\mathrm{lem{:}mass\text{-}confidence}\), applied separately to real and
imaginary parts, gives, whenever \(n_x>\lambda_n\),
\[
 \Pr\left(
 |\widehat F_{x,n}(s,t)-F_x(s,t)|
 >2\sqrt{\lambda_n/n_x}\ \middle|\ (X_i)_{i=1}^n
 \right)\le4e^{-\lambda_n},                                      \tag{1}
\]
and
\[
 \Pr\left(
 |\widehat G_{x,n}(s,t)-G_x(s,t)|
 >2B_Y\sqrt{\lambda_n/n_x}\ \middle|\ (X_i)_{i=1}^n
 \right)\le4e^{-\lambda_n}.                                     \tag{2}
\]
Indeed, if a complex number has modulus greater than \(u\), one of its real
and imaginary parts has modulus greater than \(u/\sqrt2\).  If
\(n_x\le\lambda_n\), the channel bounds and the empty-cell convention give
the defining inequalities deterministically, since then
\(\rho^F_{x,n}=2\) and \(\rho^G_{x,n}=2B_Y\).  A conditional union bound
over both channels, all cells, and all grid points gives failure probability
at most
\[
 8|\mathcal X||\mathcal D_n|e^{-\lambda_n}=\alpha/6.              \tag{3}
\]
Combining (3) with the mass-region failure probability \(\alpha/3\) in
\(\mathrm{lem{:}mass\text{-}confidence}\), then integrating over the cell
labels, proves uniformly over \(P\in\mathcal M\) that
\[
 P_{\mathrm{obs}}^{\otimes n}(\mathcal E_{n,\alpha})
 \ge1-\alpha/3-\alpha/6\ge1-\alpha.                              \tag{4}
\]

Suppose that \(\mathcal E_{n,\alpha}\) occurs.  Apply
\(\mathrm{lem{:}outer\text{-}spline\text{-}embedding}\) in every cell and
\(\mathrm{lem{:}atomic\text{-}grid\text{-}embedding}\) to both error laws,
and set
\[
 \bar\theta_n=
 \bigl((p_x,\widetilde f_{x,n},\widetilde q_{x,n})_{x\in\mathcal X},
       \bar\phi_{1,n},\bar\phi_{2,n}\bigr).                      \tag{5}
\]
The event places its mass vector in \(\mathcal P_{n,\alpha}\).  At a point
\((s,t)\in\mathcal D_n\), both \(s,t\in\Gamma_n\).  Characteristic
functions have modulus at most one.  Also \(|\widehat f_x(u)|\le1\), while
\(|q_x|\le B_Yf_x\) gives \(|\widehat q_x(u)|\le B_Y\).  Uniform spline
approximation over an interval of length \(2B_A\) gives
\[
 |\widehat{\widetilde f}_{x,n}(u)-\widehat f_x(u)|
 \le2B_Aa_{f,n},
 \qquad
 |\widehat{\widetilde q}_{x,n}(u)-\widehat q_x(u)|
 \le2B_Aa_{q,n}.                                                  \tag{6}
\]
The atomic embedding and the triangle inequality give
\[
 |\bar\phi_{1,n}(s)\bar\phi_{2,n}(t)-\phi_1(s)\phi_2(t)|
 \le2\tau_{e,n}.                                                  \tag{7}
\]
Using \(\mathrm{lem{:}factorization}\), (6)--(7), and the definitions of
the bias allowances, we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
 |\widehat{\widetilde f}_{x,n}(s+t)
   \bar\phi_{1,n}(s)\bar\phi_{2,n}(t)-F_x(s,t)|
 &\le2B_Aa_{f,n}+2\tau_{e,n}\le\delta^F_n,\\
 |\widehat{\widetilde q}_{x,n}(s+t)
   \bar\phi_{1,n}(s)\bar\phi_{2,n}(t)-G_x(s,t)|
 &\le2B_Aa_{q,n}+2B_Y\tau_{e,n}\le\delta^G_n.                   \tag{8}
\end{aligned}
\]
The empirical inequalities on \(\mathcal E_{n,\alpha}\) and (8) verify all
residual constraints in \(\mathrm{def{:}joint\text{-}feasible\text{-}set}\),
while the embedding lemmas verify all deterministic sieve constraints.
Thus
\[
 \bar\theta_n\in\Theta_{n,\alpha}.                               \tag{9}
\]
The quotient conclusion of the outer-spline embedding, using the true mass
vector, gives
\[
 \|\mu_{\bar\theta_n}-\mu\|_{L^\infty(I)}\le b_{\mu,n}.          \tag{10}
\]

It remains to prove the samplewise clipping assertions.  Put
\(e_n=a_{q,n}+B_Ya_{f,n}\).  For any
\(\theta\in\Theta_{n,\alpha}\), the simplex constraint, the marked outer
envelope, and \(f_x\ge\kappa/2\) on \(I\) imply
\[
 |\mu_\theta(a)|
 \le\sum_xp_x\left(B_Y+\frac{e_n}{f_x(a)}\right)
 \le B_Y+\frac{2e_n}{\kappa}
 =B_Y+\frac{b_{\mu,n}}2.                                         \tag{11}
\]
If the feasible set is nonempty, let
\(\ell(a)=\inf_{\theta\in\Theta_{n,\alpha}}\mu_\theta(a)\) and
\(u(a)=\sup_{\theta\in\Theta_{n,\alpha}}\mu_\theta(a)\).  From (11) and
\(\ell(a)\le u(a)\),
\[
 \ell(a)-b_{\mu,n}\le B_Y,\qquad
 -B_Y\le u(a)+b_{\mu,n},\qquad
 \ell(a)-b_{\mu,n}\le u(a)+b_{\mu,n}.                           \tag{12}
\]
Together with \(-B_Y\le B_Y\), these inequalities show that the maximum
defining \(L_n(a)\) does not exceed the minimum defining \(U_n(a)\).  Both
endpoints lie in \([-B_Y,B_Y]\).  If the feasible set is empty, both are
zero by definition.  Hence, for every sample,
\[
 L_n(a)\le U_n(a)\quad(a\in I),
 \qquad 0\le W_n\le2B_Y.                                         \tag{13}
\]
Equations (4), (9), (10), and (13) prove all assertions.

Fix \(n\) at least as large as the deterministic threshold in
\(\mathrm{lem{:}analytic\text{-}sieve\text{-}stability}\).  We first verify
measurability.  At fixed \(n\), every coefficient, weight, and atom vector
lives in a finite-dimensional Euclidean space.  If
\(f\in\mathscr F_n\) and \(f=f_+-f_-\), then the signal-sieve constraints
give
\[
 \int_{\mathcal A}f_-\le2B_Aa_{f,n},
 \qquad
 \int_{\mathcal A}f_+
 =\int_{\mathcal A}f+\int_{\mathcal A}f_-
 \le1+4B_Aa_{f,n},
\]
and consequently
\[
 \|f\|_{L^1(\mathcal A)}\le1+6B_Aa_{f,n}.                       \tag{1}
\]
For \(q\in\mathscr Q_n(f)\), its envelope yields
\[
 \|q\|_{L^1(\mathcal A)}
 \le B_Y(1+2B_Aa_{f,n})+2B_A(a_{q,n}+B_Ya_{f,n}).                \tag{2}
\]
Equivalence of norms on each fixed finite-dimensional spline space turns
(1)--(2) into coefficient bounds.  The closed signal constraints therefore
define compact coefficient sets.  The error-law constraints are closed
subsets of a product of the compact probability simplex and
\([-H_n,H_n]^{M_n}\); the moment, ordering, centering-tolerance, and
protected-modulus maps are continuous.  Hence all deterministic constraints
form a compact parameter set \(K_n^\star\).  Every density coordinate in
that set obeys
\[
 \inf_{a\in I}f_x(a)\ge\kappa/2,                                 \tag{3}
\]
so \((a,\theta)\mapsto\mu_\theta(a)\) is continuous and finite on
\(I\times K_n^\star\).

For a sample \(z\), let \(h_n(z,\theta)\) be the maximum of zero and the
positive parts of all mass and channel constraint violations, with the
deterministic constraints absorbed into \(K_n^\star\).  Then \(h_n\) is
measurable in \(z\), continuous in \(\theta\), and
\[
 \Theta_{n,\alpha}(z)=\{\theta\in K_n^\star:h_n(z,\theta)=0\}.   \tag{4}
\]
If \(K_n^\star\) is empty, the prescribed endpoints are zero.  Otherwise,
let \(K_{n,0}^\star\) be a countable dense subset.  Continuity gives
\[
 d_n(z):=\inf_{\theta\in K_n^\star}h_n(z,\theta)
       =\inf_{\theta\in K_{n,0}^\star}h_n(z,\theta),             \tag{5}
\]
so \(d_n\) is measurable; compactness and (4) show that the feasible set is
nonempty exactly when \(d_n=0\).  For positive integers \(k\), define
\[
 V_{n,k}^+(z,a)=\sup_{\theta\in K_n^\star}
 \{\mu_\theta(a)-kh_n(z,\theta)\},
 \quad
 V_{n,k}^-(z,a)=\sup_{\theta\in K_n^\star}
 \{-\mu_\theta(a)-kh_n(z,\theta)\}.                             \tag{6}
\]
Each supremum equals the supremum over \(K_{n,0}^\star\), hence is jointly
measurable.  On \(\{d_n=0\}\), compactness gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 V_{n,k}^+(z,a)&\downarrow
 \sup_{\theta\in\Theta_{n,\alpha}(z)}\mu_\theta(a),\\
 V_{n,k}^-(z,a)&\downarrow
 -\inf_{\theta\in\Theta_{n,\alpha}(z)}\mu_\theta(a).           \tag{7}
\end{aligned}
\]
To see this, compare a maximizer with any feasible point.  Boundedness of
\(\mu_\theta(a)\) forces its violation to be \(O(k^{-1})\), and every
convergent subsequence has a feasible limit by (4); feasible points give the
reverse inequality.  Equations (5)--(7), together with the empty-set
convention, prove joint sample-and-index measurability of the extrema and of
\(L_n,U_n\).  Uniform continuity on the compact product
\(I\times\Theta_{n,\alpha}(z)\) makes the profiled extrema continuous in
\(a\).  Therefore \(W_n\) is measurable because its supremum may be taken
over a fixed countable dense subset of \(I\).

The stability lemma gives for every sample
\[
 L_n(a)\le U_n(a)\quad(a\in I),
 \qquad0\le W_n\le2B_Y.                                          \tag{8}
\]
Fix \(P\in\mathcal M\).  On \(\mathcal E_{n,\alpha}\), that lemma supplies
\(\bar\theta_n\in\Theta_{n,\alpha}\) satisfying
\[
 \sup_{a\in I}|\mu_{\bar\theta_n}(a)-\mu(a)|\le b_{\mu,n}.      \tag{9}
\]
The structural response takes values in \([-B_Y,B_Y]\), so
\[
 -B_Y\le\mu(a)\le B_Y\qquad(a\in I).                             \tag{10}
\]
For every \(a\in I\), feasibility and (9) imply
\[
 \inf_{\theta\in\Theta_{n,\alpha}}\mu_\theta(a)-b_{\mu,n}
 \le\mu(a),
 \qquad
 \sup_{\theta\in\Theta_{n,\alpha}}\mu_\theta(a)+b_{\mu,n}
 \ge\mu(a).                                                       \tag{11}
\]
Equation (10) shows that clipping preserves both inequalities, whence
\[
 \mathcal E_{n,\alpha}\subseteq
 \{L_n(a)\le\mu(a)\le U_n(a)\text{ for every }a\in I\}.         \tag{12}
\]
Taking probabilities and using the uniform event bound proves
\[
 \inf_{P\in\mathcal M}P_{\mathrm{obs}}^{\otimes n}
 \{L_n(a)\le\mu(a)\le U_n(a)\text{ for every }a\in I\}
 \ge1-\alpha.                                                     \tag{13}
\]
Joint measurability, (8), and (13) are exactly the requirements of
\(\mathrm{def{:}honest\text{-}bands}\), so
\(\mathcal C_n\in\mathfrak B_{n,\alpha}\).  Finally, (8) yields
\[
 \sup_{P\in\mathcal M}E_{P_{\mathrm{obs}}^{\otimes n}}[W_n]
 \le2B_Y.                                                         \tag{14}
\]
The threshold is uniform because it is the one supplied by the stability
lemma and depends only on \(\alpha\) and the fixed class indices.

Suppose \(Y(a)=1\) almost surely for every \(a\in\mathcal A\).  By
\(\mathrm{ass{:}consistency}\), \(Y=1\) almost surely, so
\(m_x(a)=1\) for \(f_x(a)\,da\)-almost every \(a\).  Therefore
\[
 q_x(a)=m_x(a)f_x(a)=f_x(a)
\]
almost everywhere.  Since \(f_x,q_x\in H^\beta(\mathbb R)\) and
\(\beta>1/2\), their continuous Sobolev representatives coincide
everywhere.  Directly from the channel definitions,
\[
 G_x(s,t)=E[Ye^{i(sS_1+tS_2)}\mid X=x]
 =E[e^{i(sS_1+tS_2)}\mid X=x]=F_x(s,t),
\]
and the causal definition gives \(\mu(a)=E[Y(a)]=1\).

The cited \(\mathrm{lem{:}capitao\text{-}theorem\text{-}one}\) applies to
the probability channel: \(\mathrm{ass{:}compact\text{-}dose}\) supplies
its latent-signal condition (H2), and
\(\mathrm{ass{:}error\text{-}coordinate\text{-}independence}\) supplies
its coordinate-independence condition (H1).  That theorem identifies the
latent and error laws up to common translation.  In the present scalar
model, \(E_P[U_2]=0\) from \(\mathrm{ass{:}center\text{-}two}\) fixes this
translation, exactly as the derivative calculation in
\(\mathrm{thm{:}marked\text{-}cocycle\text{-}id}\) shows.  After removing
the redundant marked channel \(G_x=F_x\), this is the stated normalized
special case of their Theorem 1.

Fix \(P\in\mathcal M\), \(j\in\{1,2\}\), and a sufficiently large \(n\).
Define
\[
 U_j^H=\max\{-H_n,\min\{U_j,H_n\}\}.
\]
On \(\{|U_j|>H_n\}\), one has
\(1\le |U_j|^{q_e}H_n^{-q_e}\), so
\(\mathrm{ass{:}error\text{-}moment}\) gives
\[
 P(|U_j|>H_n)\le M_eH_n^{-q_e}.                                  \tag{1}
\]
Since \(U_j^H=U_j\) off this event and two unit-modulus complex numbers are
at distance at most two,
\[
 |E_Pe^{itU_j^H}-\phi_j(t)|
 \le2P(|U_j|>H_n)
 \le2M_eH_n^{-q_e}=\tau_{e,n}                                   \tag{2}
\]
for every real \(t\).  Clipping also gives
\[
 E_P|U_j^H|^{q_e}\le E_P|U_j|^{q_e}\le M_e.                     \tag{3}
\]
For \(j=2\), the first moment exists by
\(\mathrm{lem{:}moment\text{-}derived\text{-}local\text{-}modulus}\).
Using \(E_PU_2=0\) from \(\mathrm{ass{:}center\text{-}two}\) and
\(q_e>1\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
 |E_PU_2^H|
 &=|E_P(U_2^H-U_2)|\\
 &\le E_P[|U_2|\mathbf1\{|U_2|>H_n\}]\\
 &\le H_n^{1-q_e}E_P|U_2|^{q_e}
 \le M_eH_n^{1-q_e}.                                             \tag{4}
\end{aligned}
\]
The strict inequality \(q_e>1\) is exactly what makes this centering error
vanish as \(H_n\to\infty\).

We replace the law of \(U_j^H\), supported on \([-H_n,H_n]\), by an atomic
law preserving the grid values and the two moments.  Put
\(D=2|\Gamma_n|+2\) and define the continuous map
\[
 v(u)=\left((\operatorname{Re}e^{itu},\operatorname{Im}e^{itu})_{t\in\Gamma_n},
             u,|u|^{q_e}\right)\in\mathbb R^D.                  \tag{5}
\]
Finite simple-law approximations and uniform continuity of \(v\) show that
\(E_Pv(U_j^H)\) belongs to the closure of the convex hull of the compact set
\(v([-H_n,H_n])\).  We now show that this convex hull is closed and obtain
the needed support bound.  If a finite convex representation uses more than
\(D+1\) locations \(u_r\), the augmented vectors
\((1,v(u_r))\in\mathbb R^{D+1}\) are linearly dependent.  Hence there are
real \(a_r\), not all zero, such that
\[
 \sum_ra_r=0,\qquad \sum_ra_rv(u_r)=0.                            \tag{6}
\]
After changing signs, some \(a_r>0\).  For weights \(w_r\), let
\[
 c=\min_{r:a_r>0}\frac{w_r}{a_r}>0,
 \qquad w'_r=w_r-ca_r.
\]
The new weights are nonnegative, have the same sum and barycenter, and at
least one positive-weight location disappears.  Iteration leaves at most
\[
 D+1=2|\Gamma_n|+3\le M_n                                      \tag{7}
\]
locations.  Thus the convex hull is the continuous image of the compact
product of a \(D\)-simplex and \(D+1\) copies of \([-H_n,H_n]\), and hence
is compact and closed.  Therefore \(E_Pv(U_j^H)\) has such a representation.

Let \(\bar Q_{j,n}\) be the resulting atomic law.  Order its locations and
pad with zero-weight atoms at \(H_n\).  By (5), its characteristic function
\(\bar\phi_{j,n}\) agrees with that of \(U_j^H\) on \(\Gamma_n\), its mean
is \(E_PU_j^H\), its support is contained in \([-H_n,H_n]\), and
\[
 \int|u|^{q_e}\,d\bar Q_{j,n}(u)=E_P|U_j^H|^{q_e}\le M_e.       \tag{8}
\]
Equations (2) and (8) give
\[
 \max_{t\in\Gamma_n}|\bar\phi_{j,n}(t)-\phi_j(t)|
 \le\tau_{e,n}.                                                   \tag{9}
\]
For \(j=2\), preservation of the mean and (4) give
\[
 \left|\sum_{\ell=1}^{M_n}w_{2\ell}u_{2\ell}\right|
 \le M_eH_n^{1-q_e}\le2M_eH_n^{1-q_e}.                          \tag{10}
\]
Finally, apply
\(\mathrm{lem{:}moment\text{-}derived\text{-}local\text{-}modulus}\) to
\(\bar Q_{j,n}\), using (8).  It yields
\[
 \inf_{|t|\le\nu_*}|\bar\phi_{j,n}(t)|\ge c_*\ge c_*/2.        \tag{11}
\]
Thus (8), (11), the support restriction, and the ordered-atom construction
put \(\bar\phi_{j,n}\) in \(\widetilde\Phi_{j,n}\).  Equation (10) puts
the second coordinate in \(\Phi_{2,n}\), while
\(\Phi_{1,n}=\widetilde\Phi_{1,n}\).  Equations (9)--(10) prove the claim.

By \(\mathrm{def{:}exact\text{-}projected\text{-}class}\), every signal
coordinate is supported on \(\mathcal A=[-B_A,B_A]\), and its
\(H^\beta\)-norm is bounded by \(R_f\) or \(R_q\).  Use the Fourier norm
convention
\[
 \|g\|_{H^\beta}^2
 =\frac1{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb R}(1+t^2)^\beta|\widehat g(t)|^2\,dt.\tag{1}
\]
Fourier inversion and Cauchy--Schwarz give, first for smooth functions and
then by \(H^\beta\) approximation,
\[
 |g(a)|\le\frac{\|g\|_{H^\beta}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}
 \left\{\int_{\mathbb R}(1+t^2)^{-\beta}\,dt\right\}^{1/2},     \tag{2}
\]
and
\[
 |g(a)-g(b)|\le\frac{\|g\|_{H^\beta}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}
 \left\{\int_{\mathbb R}|e^{-ita}-e^{-itb}|^2
 (1+t^2)^{-\beta}\,dt\right\}^{1/2}.                            \tag{3}
\]
The integral in (2) is finite because \(\beta>1/2\).  The integrand in (3)
converges pointwise to zero as \(|a-b|\to0\) and is bounded by
\(4(1+t^2)^{-\beta}\).  Dominated convergence therefore provides a common
modulus of continuity for each fixed-radius Sobolev ball.  Such a ball is
uniformly bounded and equicontinuous on \(\mathcal A\).

These estimates also give total boundedness directly.  Given
\(\epsilon>0\), choose a finite mesh of \(\mathcal A\) so that (3) is at
most \(\epsilon/4\) between each point and a nearest mesh point.  Partition
the bounded range in (2) into finitely many intervals of length
\(\epsilon/2\).  Two functions with the same interval pattern on the mesh
are at uniform distance at most \(\epsilon\), so finitely many selected
representatives form an \(\epsilon\)-net.

For closedness, suppose \(g_m\) is supported in \(\mathcal A\),
\(\|g_m\|_{H^\beta}\le R\), and \(g_m\to g\) uniformly on \(\mathcal A\).
The continuous representatives vanish off \(\mathcal A\), hence also at its
boundary.  The zero extension of \(g\) is continuous and
\[
 \|g_m-g\|_{L^2(\mathbb R)}
 \le(2B_A)^{1/2}\|g_m-g\|_{L^\infty(\mathcal A)}\longrightarrow0.\tag{4}
\]
Put \(h_m(t)=(1+t^2)^{\beta/2}\widehat g_m(t)\).  Equation (1) makes
\((h_m)\) bounded in \(L^2\), so a subsequence converges weakly to some
\(h\) and
\[
 \|h\|_2\le\liminf_m\|h_m\|_2.                                  \tag{5}
\]
By (4) and the Fourier isometry,
\(\widehat g_m\to\widehat g\) strongly in \(L^2\).  On the other hand,
weak convergence of \(h_m\) implies weak convergence of
\(\widehat g_m=(1+t^2)^{-\beta/2}h_m\) to
\((1+t^2)^{-\beta/2}h\).  Uniqueness of weak limits gives
\(\widehat g=(1+t^2)^{-\beta/2}h\), so \(g\in H^\beta\) and (5) preserves
the radius.  Thus the fixed-support ball is closed in \(C(\mathcal A)\), and
total boundedness proves compactness.

Apply this at radii \(R_f\) and \(R_q\).  Uniform convergence preserves
nonnegativity, the lower bound by \(\kappa\) on \(I\), and
\(|q_x|\le B_Yf_x\).  It also preserves the unit integral because
\[
 \left|\int_{\mathcal A}(f_m-f)\right|
 \le2B_A\|f_m-f\|_{L^\infty(\mathcal A)}\longrightarrow0.        \tag{6}
\]
Hence the joint signal set is compact.  The mass vectors form a closed
subset of the finite-dimensional simplex and are compact as well.

For an error coordinate, let \((Q_m)\) satisfy the common moment bound.
Markov's inequality gives
\[
 \sup_mQ_m(|u|>R)\le M_eR^{-q_e},                                 \tag{7}
\]
so the family is tight.  A diagonal subsequence of the distribution
functions on rational arguments defines a limiting distribution function;
(7) forces its limits at the two infinities to be zero and one.  Rational
sandwiching gives convergence at every continuity point.  Approximating a
bounded continuous function on \([-R,R]\) by step functions with endpoints
at continuity points, then using (7) as \(R\to\infty\), proves weak
convergence along the subsequence to a Borel probability law \(Q\):
\[
 \int h\,dQ_m\longrightarrow\int h\,dQ
 \quad\text{for every bounded continuous }h.                     \tag{8}
\]
Apply (8) to \(|u|^{q_e}\wedge L\), then let \(L\to\infty\), to get
\[
 \int|u|^{q_e}\,dQ(u)\le M_e.                                   \tag{9}
\]
Because \(q_e>1\),
\[
 \int_{|u|>R}|u|\,dQ_m(u)
 \le M_eR^{1-q_e}\longrightarrow0                               \tag{10}
\]
uniformly in \(m\), and (9) gives the same bound for \(Q\).  Applying (8)
to the identity clipped to \([-R,R]\), then using (10), proves convergence
of first moments.  Thus the centering condition on \(Q_2\) is closed.  This
proves compactness of both error-law coordinates in any metric that
metrizes weak convergence.

The power-mean inequality also gives
\(\int|u|\,dQ_m(u)\le M_e^{1/q_e}\), whence
\[
 |\phi_{Q_m}(s)-\phi_{Q_m}(t)|
 \le |s-t|M_e^{1/q_e}.                                           \tag{11}
\]
Weak convergence gives pointwise convergence of the characteristic
functions.  A finite-mesh argument using (11) for both \(Q_m\) and \(Q\)
upgrades this to uniform convergence on every compact frequency interval.
Together with the preceding coordinatewise compactness, this proves
compactness of \(\mathscr K\).

If \(\vartheta_m\to\vartheta\) in the asserted product metric, common
support gives
\[
 \sup_{r\in\mathbb R}|\widehat f_{x,m}(r)-\widehat f_x(r)|
 \le2B_A\|f_{x,m}-f_x\|_{L^\infty(\mathcal A)}\longrightarrow0, \tag{12}
\]
and similarly for \(q_x\).  Characteristic functions have modulus at most
one, \(\int f_x=1\), and \(\int|q_x|\le B_Y\).  Thus (11)--(12) prove local
uniform convergence on \(\mathbb R^2\) of both fitted channels.

For the profiled target, if \(f_x,f'_x\ge\kappa\) and
\(|q'_x|\le B_Yf'_x\) on \(I\), then
\[
 \left\|\frac{q_x}{f_x}-\frac{q'_x}{f'_x}\right\|_{L^\infty(I)}
 \le\kappa^{-1}\|q_x-q'_x\|_{L^\infty(\mathcal A)}
   +B_Y\kappa^{-1}\|f_x-f'_x\|_{L^\infty(\mathcal A)}.         \tag{13}
\]
Also \(\|q'_x/f'_x\|_\infty\le B_Y\), and therefore
\[
 \|\mu_\vartheta-\mu_{\vartheta'}\|_{L^\infty(I)}
 \le\sum_xp_x
 \left\|\frac{q_x}{f_x}-\frac{q'_x}{f'_x}\right\|_{L^\infty(I)}
 +B_Y\sum_x|p_x-p'_x|.                                          \tag{14}
\]
This proves continuity into \(C(I)\).

Finally fix \(n\) and a sample \(z\).  Feasibility is the conjunction of
finitely many mass and channel inequalities.  A typical probability-channel
violation is
\[
 \left(
 \left|\widehat F_{x,n}(z;s,t)-
 \widehat f_x(s+t)\phi_{Q_1}(s)\phi_{Q_2}(t)\right|
 -\rho^F_{x,n}(z)
 \right)_+,                                                      \tag{15}
\]
with analogous marked and mass violations.  The empirical sums, counts,
empty-cell convention, and radii are Borel measurable in \(z\); local
uniform channel convergence and continuity of the mass coordinates make all
violations continuous in \(\vartheta\).  Their common zero set is precisely
\(\Theta^{\mathrm{ex}}_{n,\alpha}(z)\), hence is closed in compact
\(\mathscr K\) and is compact.  This proves every assertion.

Suppose, for contradiction, that \(\omega_n\not\to0\).  Then there are
\(\epsilon>0\), integers \(n_k\to\infty\), samples \(z_k\) satisfying
\(\min_xn_x(z_k)\ge n_kp_{\min}/2\), and
\(\vartheta_k,\vartheta'_k\in
\Theta^{\mathrm{ex}}_{n_k,\alpha}(z_k)\) such that
\[
 \|\mu_{\vartheta_k}-\mu_{\vartheta'_k}\|_{L^\infty(I)}
 \ge\epsilon.                                                     \tag{1}
\]
By \(\mathrm{lem{:}exact\text{-}class\text{-}compactness}\), after taking
one common subsequence,
\[
 \vartheta_k\longrightarrow\vartheta,
 \qquad \vartheta'_k\longrightarrow\vartheta'.                  \tag{2}
\]
Both mass vectors belong to the same confidence region, so
\[
 \max_x|p_{x,k}-p'_{x,k}|
 \le2\left\{\frac{\log(6|\mathcal X|/\alpha)}{2n_k}\right\}^{1/2}
 \longrightarrow0.                                               \tag{3}
\]
Thus the limiting mass vectors agree.

The grid definition gives
\[
 |\mathcal D_n|=(2K_n^2+1)^2,
 \qquad \lambda_n=O(\log K_n)=o(n).                              \tag{4}
\]
Consequently, on these regular-count samples,
\[
 \max_x\rho^F_{x,n_k}
 \le2\left(\frac{2\lambda_{n_k}}{n_kp_{\min}}\right)^{1/2}=o(1),
 \qquad
 \max_x\rho^G_{x,n_k}\le B_Y\max_x\rho^F_{x,n_k}=o(1).         \tag{5}
\]
For a tuple \(\vartheta\), abbreviate its fitted channels by
\[
 F_{x,\vartheta}(s,t)=
 \widehat f_x(s+t)\phi_{Q_1}(s)\phi_{Q_2}(t),
 \quad
 G_{x,\vartheta}(s,t)=
 \widehat q_x(s+t)\phi_{Q_1}(s)\phi_{Q_2}(t).                    \tag{6}
\]
The moment bound and the power-mean inequality give
\(\int|u|\,dQ_j(u)\le M_e^{1/q_e}\).  Since \(|a|\le B_A\) on
\(\mathcal A\), \(|e^{iv}-e^{iw}|\le|v-w|\), and
\(\int|q_x|\le B_Y\), direct integration gives, uniformly in
\(\vartheta\in\mathscr K\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
 |F_{x,\vartheta}(s,t)-F_{x,\vartheta}(s',t')|
 &\le(B_A+M_e^{1/q_e})(|s-s'|+|t-t'|),\\
 |G_{x,\vartheta}(s,t)-G_{x,\vartheta}(s',t')|
 &\le B_Y(B_A+M_e^{1/q_e})(|s-s'|+|t-t'|).                       \tag{7}
\end{aligned}
\]
At each grid point, feasibility of both tuples around the same empirical
channels gives
\[
 |F_{x,\vartheta_k}-F_{x,\vartheta'_k}|\le2\rho^F_{x,n_k},
 \qquad
 |G_{x,\vartheta_k}-G_{x,\vartheta'_k}|\le2\rho^G_{x,n_k}.       \tag{8}
\]
The mesh of \(\Gamma_{n_k}\) is \((B_AK_{n_k})^{-1}\), while its range is
\(K_{n_k}/B_A\to\infty\).  For each fixed \((s,t)\), choose a nearest
grid point for all large \(k\).  Equations (5), (7), and (8) show that the
two fitted probability channels, and separately the two marked channels,
approach one another at \((s,t)\).  The local uniform convergence from the
compactness lemma permits passage to (2), giving
\[
 F_{x,\vartheta}(s,t)=F_{x,\vartheta'}(s,t),
 \qquad
 G_{x,\vartheta}(s,t)=G_{x,\vartheta'}(s,t)                       \tag{9}
\]
for all \(x,s,t\).

We next derive local nonvanishing from the moment constraint.  For every
candidate error law,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 |\phi_Q(v)|
 &\ge1-|\phi_Q(v)-1|\\
 &\ge1-\int|e^{ivu}-1|\,dQ(u)\\
 &\ge1-|v|\int|u|\,dQ(u)
 \ge1-|v|M_e^{1/q_e}.                                            \tag{10}
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus \(|\phi_Q(v)|\ge c_*=1/2\) for
\(|v|\le\nu_*=(2M_e^{1/q_e})^{-1}\).  Also
\[
 |\widehat f_x(v)-1|
 \le\int_{\mathcal A}|e^{iva}-1|f_x(a)\,da
 \le B_A|v|.                                                      \tag{11}
\]
Set \(\delta=\min\{(4B_A)^{-1},\nu_*/2\}>0\).  Equations (10)--(11)
make every factor of \(F_{x,\vartheta}(u,t)\) and
\(F_{x,\vartheta'}(u,t)\) nonzero whenever \(|u|,|t|\le\delta\).

Fix \(x\), and write the signal coordinates of \(\vartheta'\) as
\(\widetilde f_x,\widetilde q_x\).  Because \(q_e>1\), both
second-coordinate error laws have finite first moments.  Their centering in
the exact class gives
\[
 \phi'_{Q_2}(0)=i\int u\,dQ_2(u)=0,
 \qquad
 \phi'_{Q'_2}(0)=i\int u\,dQ'_2(u)=0.                             \tag{12}
\]
Differentiate the first equality in (9) with respect to \(t\) at
\((u,0)\), divide by the common nonzero channel, and use (12).  Then
\[
 \frac{\widehat f'_x(u)}{\widehat f_x(u)}
 =\frac{\widehat{\widetilde f}'_x(u)}{\widehat{\widetilde f}_x(u)},
 \qquad |u|\le\delta.                                            \tag{13}
\]
The ratio \(\widehat f_x/\widehat{\widetilde f}_x\) has zero derivative and
equals one at zero, so
\[
 \widehat f_x(u)=\widehat{\widetilde f}_x(u),
 \qquad |u|\le\delta.                                            \tag{14}
\]
Compact support makes both transforms entire: all differentiated integrands
are bounded using \(|a|\le B_A\) and
\(|e^{iza}|\le e^{B_A|\operatorname{Im}z|}\).  Applied to their difference,
(14) makes every Taylor coefficient at zero vanish, hence the transforms
agree on all of \(\mathbb C\).

To verify Fourier injectivity directly, let
\(h=f_x-\widetilde f_x\), and let \(\gamma_\sigma\) be the centered Gaussian
density with variance \(\sigma^2\).  Fubini's theorem and the Gaussian
integral give
\[
 (h*\gamma_\sigma)(a)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb R}
 e^{-ita}\widehat h(t)e^{-\sigma^2t^2/2}\,dt=0.                  \tag{15}
\]
Translation continuity in \(L^1\) gives
\[
 \|h*\gamma_\sigma-h\|_1
 \le\int\gamma_\sigma(y)\|h(\cdot-y)-h\|_1\,dy\longrightarrow0.\tag{16}
\]
Thus \(f_x=\widetilde f_x\) almost everywhere, and hence everywhere for
their continuous \(H^\beta\) representatives.

For \(|u|\le\delta\), equations (9) and (14), with the nonzero denominator,
give
\[
 \widehat q_x(u)
 =\widehat f_x(u)\frac{G_{x,\vartheta}(u,0)}{F_{x,\vartheta}(u,0)}
 =\widehat{\widetilde f}_x(u)
   \frac{G_{x,\vartheta'}(u,0)}{F_{x,\vartheta'}(u,0)}
 =\widehat{\widetilde q}_x(u).                                   \tag{17}
\]
The domination \(|q_x|\le B_Yf_x\) makes both signed functions integrable,
and compact support makes their transforms entire.  The analytic-continuation
and Gaussian-convolution arguments in (14)--(16) therefore give
\(q_x=\widetilde q_x\).  This holds in every cell.  Together with (3), the
limiting tuples have the same target function.

Finally, continuity of \(\vartheta\mapsto\mu_\vartheta\) and (2) give
\[
 \|\mu_{\vartheta_k}-\mu_{\vartheta'_k}\|_{L^\infty(I)}
 \longrightarrow
 \|\mu_\vartheta-\mu_{\vartheta'}\|_{L^\infty(I)}=0,
\]
contradicting (1).  Hence \(\omega_n\to0\).  The argument is qualitative
and supplies neither a numerical modulus nor an \(O(r_n)\) bound.

By \(\mathrm{lem{:}exact\text{-}class\text{-}compactness}\),
\(\mathscr K\) is a compact metric space.  If it is empty, every exact
feasible set is empty and the endpoints are identically zero, so all
measurability and width assertions are immediate and coverage over
\(\mathcal M\) is vacuous.  Assume henceforth that \(\mathscr K\ne\varnothing\).
Let \(h(z,\vartheta)\) be the maximum of zero and the positive parts of all
mass and channel violations defining
\(\Theta^{\mathrm{ex}}_{n,\alpha}(z)\).  It is measurable in \(z\),
continuous in \(\vartheta\), and
\[
 \Theta^{\mathrm{ex}}_{n,\alpha}(z)
 =\{\vartheta\in\mathscr K:h(z,\vartheta)=0\}.                    \tag{1}
\]
For a countable dense set \(K_0\subset\mathscr K\),
\[
 d(z):=\inf_{\vartheta\in\mathscr K}h(z,\vartheta)
      =\inf_{\vartheta\in K_0}h(z,\vartheta),                    \tag{2}
\]
so \(d\) is measurable, and compactness shows that the feasible set is
nonempty exactly when \(d=0\).  On that event, define
\[
 V_m^+(z,a)=\sup_{\vartheta\in\mathscr K}
 \{\mu_\vartheta(a)-mh(z,\vartheta)\},
 \quad
 V_m^-(z,a)=\sup_{\vartheta\in\mathscr K}
 \{-\mu_\vartheta(a)-mh(z,\vartheta)\}.                           \tag{3}
\]
Each supremum may be taken over \(K_0\), and is therefore jointly measurable.
Compactness and continuity imply
\[
\begin{aligned}
 V_m^+(z,a)&\downarrow
 \sup_{\vartheta\in\Theta^{\mathrm{ex}}_{n,\alpha}(z)}
 \mu_\vartheta(a),\\
 V_m^-(z,a)&\downarrow
 -\inf_{\vartheta\in\Theta^{\mathrm{ex}}_{n,\alpha}(z)}
 \mu_\vartheta(a).                                               \tag{4}
\end{aligned}
\]
Indeed, comparison with a feasible point forces a maximizing sequence's
violation to be \(O(m^{-1})\); every convergent subsequence then has a
feasible limit, and feasible points give the reverse inequalities.
Equations (2)--(4), the empty-set convention, and clipping prove joint
measurability of both endpoints.  Target continuity from the compactness
lemma makes the unprofiled extrema continuous in \(a\); hence
\(W_n^{\mathrm{ex}}\) is measurable because its supremum may be taken over a
fixed countable dense subset of \(I\).

Every \(\vartheta\in\mathscr K\) satisfies \(|q_x/f_x|\le B_Y\) on \(I\),
and its masses form a simplex.  Thus
\[
 |\mu_\vartheta(a)|\le B_Y.                                      \tag{5}
\]
Consequently clipping preserves endpoint ordering for a nonempty feasible
set, and the empty-set convention does so otherwise.  The endpoints are
finite and
\[
 0\le W_n^{\mathrm{ex}}\le2B_Y                                  \tag{6}
\]
for every sample.

Fix \(P\in\mathcal M\).  Its projected tuple
\[
 \vartheta_P=
 \bigl((p_x,f_x,q_x)_{x\in\mathcal X},
       \mathcal L_P(U_1),\mathcal L_P(U_2)\bigr)                  \tag{7}
\]
belongs to \(\mathscr K\).  The mass, support, Sobolev, denominator, moment,
and centering requirements are the corresponding member conditions of
\(\mathrm{def{:}model\text{-}class}\).  Consistency and the bounded
structural response imply \(|m_x|\le B_Y\) almost everywhere, so
\(|q_x|\le B_Yf_x\) almost everywhere and hence everywhere for the
continuous representatives.  Support of \(q_x\) follows from support of
\(f_x\).

On \(\mathcal E_{n,\alpha}\), the true mass vector belongs to
\(\mathcal P_{n,\alpha}\), and the exact identities in
\(\mathrm{lem{:}factorization}\) turn the empirical inequalities in that
event into the residual inequalities defining the exact feasible set.
Therefore
\[
 \mathcal E_{n,\alpha}
 \subseteq\{\vartheta_P\in\Theta^{\mathrm{ex}}_{n,\alpha}\}.    \tag{8}
\]
The ADRF identification theorem gives \(\mu=\mu_{\vartheta_P}\) on \(I\).
Equations (5) and (8) show that profiling and clipping contain \(\mu(a)\)
simultaneously for every \(a\in I\).  For all sufficiently large \(n\),
\(\mathrm{lem{:}analytic\text{-}sieve\text{-}stability}\) gives
\[
 \inf_{P\in\mathcal M}P_{\mathrm{obs}}^{\otimes n}
 (\mathcal E_{n,\alpha})\ge1-\alpha.                              \tag{9}
\]
Thus the exact band has uniform simultaneous coverage; the measurability,
ordering, and finiteness already proved verify every clause of
\(\mathrm{def{:}honest\text{-}bands}\).

Let \(R_n=\{\min_xn_x\ge np_{\min}/2\}\).  On \(R_n\), an empty feasible
set has zero width, while a nonempty set has width bounded by the diameter
in the definition of \(\omega_n\).  Hence
\[
 W_n^{\mathrm{ex}}\mathbf1_{R_n}\le\omega_n.                    \tag{10}
\]
On \(R_n^c\), use (6).  The count inequality in
\(\mathrm{lem{:}mass\text{-}confidence}\) and (10) give, uniformly over
\(P\in\mathcal M\),
\[
 E_{P_{\mathrm{obs}}^{\otimes n}}[W_n^{\mathrm{ex}}]
 \le\omega_n+2B_Y|\mathcal X|e^{-np_{\min}/8}.                   \tag{11}
\]
The qualitative diameter lemma gives \(\omega_n\to0\), and the exponential
term also tends to zero.  Thus the displayed bound is \(o(1)\), without any
claim of an explicit rate.

Assume the affirmative resolution stated in the hypothesis.  Consequently, there are constants \(\eta\in(0,1-2\alpha)\), \(c_{\mathrm{sep}}>0\), and \(n_0<\infty\) such that, for every \(n\ge n_0\), the two full-data laws \(P_{0,n},P_{1,n}\) belong to \(\mathcal M\) and, on defining their \(n\)-sample observed laws by
\[
Q_{j,n}:=((P_{j,n})_{\mathrm{obs}})^{\otimes n},\qquad j\in\{0,1\},
\]
one has
\[
\operatorname{TV}(Q_{0,n},Q_{1,n})\le \eta,
\qquad
\Delta_n:=\|\mu_{1,n}-\mu_{0,n}\|_{L^\infty(I)}
\ge c_{\mathrm{sep}}K_n^{1/2-\beta}.
\tag{1}
\]
These are exactly the membership, contiguity, and separation conclusions in the affirmative resolution; the i.i.d. sampling assumption identifies \(Q_{j,n}\) as the relevant sample law.

Fix \(n\ge n_0\) and an arbitrary band \(\mathcal C_n=(L_n,U_n)\in\mathfrak B_{n,\alpha}\).  For \(j\in\{0,1\}\), let
\[
H_{j,n}:=\bigl\{L_n(a)\le \mu_{j,n}(a)\le U_n(a)
                  \text{ for every }a\in I\bigr\}.
\tag{2}
\]
These are the coverage events appearing in the definition of \(\mathfrak B_{n,\alpha}\).  Since \(P_{j,n}\in\mathcal M\), uniform honesty gives
\[
Q_{j,n}(H_{j,n})\ge 1-\alpha,
\qquad j\in\{0,1\}.
\tag{3}
\]
By the defining variational inequality for total variation, \(Q_{0,n}(E)\ge Q_{1,n}(E)-\operatorname{TV}(Q_{0,n},Q_{1,n})\) for every measurable event \(E\).  Applying this with \(E=H_{1,n}\), and then using (1) and (3), yields
\[
Q_{0,n}(H_{1,n})
\ge Q_{1,n}(H_{1,n})-\operatorname{TV}(Q_{0,n},Q_{1,n})
\ge 1-\alpha-\eta.
\tag{4}
\]
The union bound, (3), and (4) therefore imply
\[
Q_{0,n}(H_{0,n}\cap H_{1,n})
\ge 1-Q_{0,n}(H_{0,n}^{c})-Q_{0,n}(H_{1,n}^{c})
\ge 1-2\alpha-\eta.
\tag{5}
\]
On \(H_{0,n}\cap H_{1,n}\), the interval \([L_n(a),U_n(a)]\) contains both \(\mu_{0,n}(a)\) and \(\mu_{1,n}(a)\) for every \(a\in I\).  Hence, pointwise in \(a\),
\[
U_n(a)-L_n(a)\ge |\mu_{1,n}(a)-\mu_{0,n}(a)|,
\]
and the definition of \(W_n\) gives
\[
W_n\ge \Delta_n
\quad\text{on }H_{0,n}\cap H_{1,n}.
\tag{6}
\]
Moreover, \(W_n\ge0\) almost surely by the definition of \(\mathfrak B_{n,\alpha}\).  Combining (1), (5), and (6),
\[
E_{Q_{0,n}}[W_n]
\ge \Delta_n Q_{0,n}(H_{0,n}\cap H_{1,n})
\ge (1-2\alpha-\eta)c_{\mathrm{sep}}K_n^{1/2-\beta}.
\tag{7}
\]
This calculation is the two-point expected-length argument recorded in the stated Low lemma.  Put
\[
c':=(1-2\alpha-\eta)c_{\mathrm{sep}}.
\]
The restriction \(\eta<1-2\alpha\) and the inequality \(c_{\mathrm{sep}}>0\) imply \(c'>0\).  Because \(P_{0,n}\in\mathcal M\), (7) entails, for every \(\mathcal C_n\in\mathfrak B_{n,\alpha}\),
\[
\sup_{P\in\mathcal M}E_{P_{\mathrm{obs}}^{\otimes n}}[W_n]
\ge E_{Q_{0,n}}[W_n]
\ge c'K_n^{1/2-\beta}.
\]
Taking the infimum over \(\mathcal C_n\in\mathfrak B_{n,\alpha}\) proves the first asserted inequality.

It remains to verify the displayed scale equivalence under the current smoothness range.  Let
\[
x_n:=\frac{\log n}{\log\log n},
\qquad
\gamma:=\beta-\frac12.
\]
The assumption \(\beta>1/2\) gives \(\gamma>0\).  For all sufficiently large \(n\), \(x_n\ge2\) and the definition \(K_n=\lfloor x_n\rfloor\) implies
\[
\frac{x_n}{2}\le K_n\le x_n.
\]
Since \(u\mapsto u^{-\gamma}\) is decreasing on \((0,\infty)\),
\[
x_n^{-\gamma}\le K_n^{-\gamma}\le 2^\gamma x_n^{-\gamma}.
\tag{8}
\]
Finally,
\[
x_n^{-\gamma}
=\left(\frac{\log\log n}{\log n}\right)^{\beta-1/2}
=r_n.
\tag{9}
\]
Equations (8)--(9) show \(K_n^{1/2-\beta}\asymp r_n\).  Increasing \(n_0\), if necessary, to a finite \(n_1\) for which the definition of \(K_n\) and the preceding bounds all hold completes the conditional proof.
